GANBOS 2 Costa Rica - Huetar Norte Test Site  |  Prepared 07 April 2026  |  Screening layers T1 through T6

Site Overview: GANBOS 2 Costa Rica - Huetar Norte Test Site

Isthmian-Atlantic moist forests (Tropical & Subtropical Moist Broadleaf Forests, Neotropic realm). Forest mosaic under active land conversion pressure: 78% forest at 30 m (GLC_FCS30D, trend -0.35%/yr) with 18% cropland encroachment. T3 (1 km HILDA+) records 88% persistent non-forest (scale artefact of majority classification in mixed forest-agriculture pixels; not evidence of full conversion). NCS reforestation eligible: 70%. Albedo offset: -15.3% median (expected tropical moist forest warming offset; not material at this magnitude). IPLC: no features within 20 km (GREEN).

T1 - Project Area

The project boundary is loaded from the supplied KML file and used as-is, with no rectangular bounding box approximation is applied. Area is computed in the EPSG:6933 World Equal-Area projection to avoid the distortion that comes from measuring area directly in degrees at tropical latitudes. The geometry is validated as a simple, non-self-intersecting polygon before any downstream analysis. All raster layers (T3-T5) are masked to this exact polygon shape.

T2 - Ecological Identity (RESOLVE Ecoregions, Dinerstein et al. 2017)

The project boundary is intersected with the RESOLVE 2017 terrestrial ecoregion dataset to establish native vegetation context and biogeographic realm. Each intersecting ecoregion is weighted by its intersection area. Biome percentages are the sum of all ecoregion areas sharing the same biome classification. Detailed assumptions and implementation choices are in the Key Assumptions table below.

Key Assumptions

Author Assumptions (Dinerstein et al. 2017) Our Implementation Choices
847 terrestrial ecoregions defined by species distribution data rather than political boundaries. Boundaries reflect long-term biogeographic patterns established over geological timescales. The RESOLVE shapefile is used in its native EPSG:4326 projection. Intersection areas are computed after reprojecting to EPSG:6933 (equal-area) to ensure accurate km² values. Percentages are derived from these equal-area intersection results.
The 14-biome and 8-realm classification is a static representation. It reflects historical vegetation patterns, not current land use or recent degradation. An ecoregion classified as tropical moist broadleaf forest may contain heavily degraded or converted land. RESOLVE biome assignment is used as a proxy for native vegetation context, not current state. Current forest cover trajectories are assessed independently in T3 using Estoque et al. 2022. The two layers are complementary and should be read together. A dedicated LULC layer will be added in a later iteration to assess current conditions directly.
Ecoregion boundaries are drawn at a global scale. At sub-regional scales, the boundaries carry inherent positional uncertainty, and small percentages near edges should be treated cautiously. The dominant biome is determined by the largest intersection area. Ecoregions contributing less than 1% of area are reported but given low interpretive weight.

T3 - Forest Cover Trajectories, 1960 to 2019 (Estoque et al. 2022, HILDA+)

This layer is derived from two sources: HILDA+ (Winkler et al. 2021), a global land use change dataset at 1 km resolution, processed and classified by Estoque et al. 2022. HILDA+ records land cover state at 7 decadal snapshots: 1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2019. Each 1 km pixel is assigned a trajectory label based on how its forest/non-forest state changed (or did not change) across all 7 snapshots.

What "persistent" and "non-persistent" mean: read this before interpreting results.
  • Persistent forest: classified as forest at every one of the 7 snapshots. The pixel has been continuously forested throughout the full 60-year observation window. High confidence of stable, long-established forest cover.
  • Persistent non-forest: classified as non-forest at every one of the 7 snapshots. The pixel has never been recorded as forest in 60 years of observation. Interpretation depends on biome context: in grassland and savanna biomes, persistent non-forest is the expected natural state. In forest biomes (as here), it indicates that a non-forest cover class dominated each 1 km pixel across all seven snapshots, consistent with long-established cropland, pasture, or other modified land. HILDA+ applies majority classification at 1 km: sub-pixel forest patches covering less than half of a pixel are counted as non-forest and are not reported separately.
  • Non-persistent forest loss: was forest at some snapshot, non-forest by 2019. This is the primary deforestation signal and the key additionality risk flag for tree-planting projects. Includes losses from 2010-2019.
  • Non-persistent forest gain: was non-forest at some snapshot, forest by 2019. Captures natural regeneration or plantation establishment.
  • Non-persistent forest: forest in 1960 and 2019, with non-forest episodes in between. Temporary disturbance with recovery.
  • Non-persistent non-forest: non-forest in 1960 and 2019, with forest episodes in between. Ephemeral tree cover, possibly transitional or agroforestry.
Important caveat: HILDA+ "non-forest" is a broad class that includes agricultural land, pasture, shrubland, savanna, and wetland; it does not distinguish natural non-forest from human-modified land. High persistent non-forest in this screen is therefore ambiguous without T2 context: in a Grasslands/Savannas biome (T2), it reflects natural baseline; in a Tropical Moist Forest biome (T2), it may indicate long-standing degradation. T2 and T3 must always be interpreted together.

Key Assumptions

Author Assumptions (Estoque et al. 2022, HILDA+) Our Implementation Choices
The underlying data is HILDA+ (Winkler et al. 2021): a global land use change product at 1 km resolution in the Eckert IV projection (ESRI:54012). It covers 7 decadal snapshots: 1960, 1970, 1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, and 2019. We reproject the project boundary polygon into the raster's native Eckert IV CRS before clipping. The raster itself is never warped or resampled. The nodata value is 255 and is excluded from all statistics via masked array conventions.
128 unique pixel values encode all possible trajectory sequences across the 7 snapshots. A companion value attribute table (VAT) maps these 128 codes to 6 broad labels: persistent forest, persistent non-forest, persistent forest gain, persistent forest loss, non-persistent forest, and non-persistent non-forest. This mapping is embedded in the published dataset. We read the VAT dynamically from the ZIP archive using the same decoding logic applied to the Griscom raster. Category percentages are aggregated from all pixel values belonging to each label, not from raw pixel value comparisons.
The category "non-persistent forest loss" captures all pixels where forest was recorded at some point between 1960 and 2019 and non-forest was recorded by 2019. This includes relatively recent losses from 2010 to 2019. Uncertainty is highest in cropland and pasture-dominated areas where transitions are frequent. The 1 km resolution means that sub-kilometre scale deforestation events may not be captured. All 8 trajectory categories are reported without further aggregation. Flag thresholds are biome-aware: in a forest biome, persistent non-forest above 60% is flagged AMBER (non-forest majority class dominance at 1 km resolution); in a grassland/savanna biome, persistent non-forest above 50% is noted as a natural baseline (not degradation). True polygon masking is used throughout — pixels are counted only if their centres fall inside the project boundary polygon, not the bounding envelope.

AMBER: Non-forest dominant at 1 km within a forest biome.
88.2% of pixels are classified as persistent non-forest by HILDA+, meaning non-forest was the majority class in each 1 km pixel across all seven decadal snapshots (1960–2019). This does not imply absence of forest at finer scales: sub-pixel forest patches covering less than half of a 1 km pixel are captured under the non-forest majority label and not counted here. The 6.7% non-persistent forest loss records pixels that shifted from forest-majority to non-forest-majority during the observation window. Primary intervention rationale: avoided deforestation within a Tropical & Subtropical Moist Broadleaf Forests biome. Cross-reference with T3b for fine-resolution composition and the scale reconciliation note below.
T3 ↔ T3b: scale and classification reconciliation.
Why do T3 and T3b appear to diverge? T3 (1 km HILDA+) records 88% persistent non-forest; T3b (30 m GLC_FCS30D) reports 78% mean forest cover post-2000. These figures describe different properties and should not be read as contradictory. HILDA+ uses majority classification: each 1 km pixel receives a single forest or non-forest label based on the dominant land cover within that pixel. A pixel that is 55% cropland and 45% closed-canopy forest is labelled "non-forest"; the minority forest component is not counted. GLC_FCS30D resolves each 30 m cell independently, capturing forest patches that fall below the HILDA+ majority threshold. The two datasets therefore describe different properties: T3 measures land-cover dominance at landscape scale; T3b measures land-cover composition at parcel scale. This parcel is a mosaic of closed evergreen broadleaf forest (77% of the 30 m signal, code 52) interspersed with cropland (18% mean post-2000). In many 1 km neighbourhoods cropland is the majority class, producing a persistent non-forest label in HILDA+ while substantial forest cover remains at 30 m resolution. Both datasets are correct for what they measure.

Project implications. Forest cover is declining at 0.35%/yr as cropland expands. The primary intervention rationale is avoided deforestation: protecting the remaining 78% forest from continued agricultural encroachment within a Tropical & Subtropical Moist Broadleaf Forests biome. A secondary rationale is restoration of already-converted cropland patches. The dominant land-use signal is ongoing forest conversion, not a cleared or degraded baseline awaiting restoration.

T3b - Fine-Resolution Land Cover Validation (GLC_FCS30D Landsat 30m, 1985-2022)

Why T3b exists alongside T3. T3 (Estoque/HILDA+) answers the question: what is the long-run forest/non-forest persistence signal? It operates at 1 km resolution over a 60-year window and is authoritative for trajectory classification. T3b answers a different, complementary question: what finer-resolution land-cover composition supports or complicates that signal? GLC_FCS30D (Liu et al. 2020) provides 30 m Landsat-derived land cover classifications at 26 time steps from 1985 to 2022. It characterises the composition of land cover classes within the parcel boundary, distinguishes grassland from pasture/cropland from remnant forest, and detects trends that may not be visible at 1 km. The two layers are not redundant: T3 is the persistence signal; T3b is the composition and trend validation.

AMBER: Forest cover present but declining.
Mean forest cover post-2000 is 78.4%, above the dataset's GREEN threshold (50%), with a trend of -0.35%/yr. Code 52 (77% of forest signal) indicates substantial closed-canopy broadleaf forest, consistent with the Tropical & Subtropical Moist Broadleaf Forests biome baseline. Cropland is the dominant non-forest class (18% mean post-2000), consistent with active agricultural encroachment into a moist forest biome. The declining trend is the primary risk signal: forest area is contracting within the project boundary at the 30 m observation scale, and this trajectory should be verified against recent high-resolution imagery to confirm whether clearing is active, historical, or partially recovered. This signal is relevant to additionality framing: halting active clearing and protecting remaining forest is a legitimate intervention pathway in a landscape with significant residual forest cover.

T4 - NCS Reforestation Opportunity (Griscom et al. 2017)

The Griscom NCS reforestation map identifies land that is biophysically capable of supporting forest and where forests were historically present, but where the current cover is non-forest. The map explicitly excludes reforestation in areas "where forests are not the native cover type," citing biodiversity harm from tree planting in native grassy biomes (Methods; citing Veldman et al. 2015, Tyranny of trees in grassy biomes). This safeguard is encoded in the raster itself: pixels in native non-forest biomes carry NCS_Refor = 0 by design. This layer does not assess economic or political feasibility; it is a biophysical filter only.

Key Assumptions

Author Assumptions (Griscom et al. 2017) Our Implementation Choices
Reforestation opportunity is defined as areas that are currently non-forest, were historically forested, and are biophysically capable of supporting forest. Opportunity here refers to biophysical suitability only. Economic feasibility, land tenure, and political context are outside the scope of this dataset. We clip the raster to the project boundary polygon and decode all pixel values via the companion VAT DBF file (19,506 entries, columns: Value, Count, NCS_Refor). Pixel values are encoded integers in the 10,000-range and must be decoded through the VAT. Direct comparison to raw integer values produces incorrect results and was a bug in an earlier version of this code.
The map explicitly excludes reforestation in areas "where forests are not the native cover type," citing biodiversity harm from tree planting in native grassy biomes (Methods; citing Veldman et al. 2015, Tyranny of trees in grassy biomes). This safeguard is encoded in the raster itself: pixels in native non-forest biomes carry NCS_Refor = 0 by design. RESOLVE biome names are used as a separate contextualisation layer alongside this result. When the dominant biome is a grassland or savanna type, low NCS overlap is noted as an expected outcome of the Griscom safeguard rather than a data problem. The principle is Griscom's; the mapping of RESOLVE biome names to interpret the result is our implementation choice.
Raster resolution is approximately 739 m in the World Cylindrical Equal Area projection (ESRI:54034). The dataset is a global-scale product and should not be used as the sole basis for site-level reforestation suitability. Local assessments are required to confirm biophysical conditions at project scale. We reproject the project boundary polygon into the raster's native ESRI:54034 CRS before clipping. 0% of pixels within the project boundary polygon were absent from the VAT, confirming full decode coverage for this site.

T5 - Albedo Climate Implications (Hasler et al. 2024)

Land cover change alters how much sunlight a surface reflects (its albedo). In some landscapes, this biophysical effect can partially or fully offset the carbon sequestration benefit of reforestation. The Hasler dataset quantifies this albedo offset as a percentage of the carbon benefit: a value of -50% means the albedo warming effect would halve the net climate benefit, and a value of -100% means the intervention would be net climate-negative despite its carbon uptake. This layer is critical for understanding whether a given intervention is truly climate-positive when all radiative effects are considered.

Tropical context note: In tropical moist forest biomes, reforestation typically produces a moderate negative albedo offset (darker canopy vs. open pasture). This is an expected biophysical trade-off, not a project-specific risk flag. Values in the 0% to -50% range reflect a partial offset of the carbon benefit, generally outweighed by carbon sequestration gains in tropical contexts. The offset becomes material only when it exceeds -50% (substantial) or -100% (net climate-negative).

Key Assumptions

Author Assumptions (Hasler et al. 2024) Our Implementation Choices
Values represent the albedo radiative forcing offset expressed as a percentage of the carbon sequestration benefit for the same land cover transition. Positive values indicate a cooling co-benefit from albedo change; negative values indicate a warming penalty that reduces the net climate value of the intervention. We use the composite file, which assigns each pixel the most likely open-to-vegetation transition type based on the surrounding landscape context. This is the appropriate choice for a screening-level assessment where the specific intervention type has not yet been decided. Project-specific analysis should use the single-transition files (e.g., GRA2FOR, GRA2SAV) once the intervention pathway is defined.
The composite map is not transition-specific. Pixel values reflect the expected dominant transition for that landscape context, not a user-specified intervention. Uncertainty is highest in heterogeneous landscapes near biome boundaries where multiple transition types are plausible. Pixels with absolute values at or above 10,000 are treated as undefined and excluded from all statistics. This follows the Hasler paper convention for flagging extreme or undefined transition scenarios. The raster carries no formal nodata attribute, so this cap-based masking is the primary nodata filter.
The dataset covers global land areas at 0.005-degree resolution (approximately 500 m at the equator) in EPSG:4326. The analysis accounts for radiative forcing from albedo change but does not include other biophysical effects such as evapotranspiration changes or surface roughness effects, which can also influence local and regional climate. Statistics are computed over all valid (non-capped) pixels within the boundary polygon. We report the median offset, the percent of pixels in each severity bucket, and whether any net climate-negative pixels are present. The spatial map uses a diverging blue-red colormap (blue = cooling, red = warming) clipped at +/-100% for display; values between +/-100% and +/-10,000 are still included in statistics but appear at the color extreme.

T6 - IPLC Land Proximity Screen (LandMark Global Platform v202509)

This screen checks whether the project parcel overlaps with or is within 20 km of any mapped Indigenous Peoples’ or Local Community (IPLC) land as recorded in the LandMark Global Platform (September 2025 release). Two polygon layers are screened: the IPLC layer (124,616 territories with documented or customary-tenure status, sourced from national registries and indigenous-data partnerships including ANT Colombia and Wataniba/RAISG) and the Indicative layer (17,539 estimated or undemarcated territories); distance values are nearest-edge, not centroid-to-centroid.

Flag thresholds:
  • RED: direct overlap with any IPLC or Indicative polygon. FPIC required under ILO Convention 169 / Costa Rican Law 7316/1993, regardless of overlap area.
  • AMBER: nearest IPLC boundary within 20 km, no direct overlap.
  • GREEN: no IPLC features within 20 km.

Key Assumptions

Data source and dataset assumptions (LandMark v202509) Our implementation choices
LandMark does not claim to be exhaustive. Oral traditions, seasonal use areas, and territories not yet mapped or submitted to the platform will not appear. Absence of a feature in LandMark confirms only the absence of a mapped record at this dataset version. We report this screen as a minimum floor, not a ceiling. If the developer holds local stakeholder information indicating additional communities, that information should be layered on top of this screen in the ESDD.
The area_gis field in the IPLC layer stores territory area in hectares. This was verified by comparing stored values against UTM-computed polygon geometry area for known reference features. Small discrepancies are attributable to boundary version differences between the LandMark polygon and other cadastral records. We display area_gis as-is in hectares. We do not recompute territory areas; territory area reporting is secondary to overlap and distance classification.
The 20 km buffer is a precautionary standard screening distance, consistent with IFC Performance Standard 7 guidance and Equator Principles EP4. It is not a legal threshold; project-specific ESDD may warrant a different zone based on activity type, topography, and hydrology. We apply the 20 km default consistently. The buffer is constructed in UTM metric space and reprojected to EPSG:4326 for display. The same UTM zone (EPSG:32616) is used throughout T1-T6 for spatial consistency.

GREEN — no IPLC features within proximity buffer.
No IPLC features were identified within the 20 km buffer based on the LandMark dataset (v202509, Rights and Resources Initiative). This reduces immediate tenure risk signals for the current screening stage. However, absence of a mapped feature does not confirm absence of local or customary land claims: LandMark does not claim to be exhaustive, and oral-tradition territories, seasonal use areas, and unregistered community lands will not appear. If local stakeholder engagement surfaces additional communities within the project area, that information should be layered on top of this screen in the Environmental and Social Due Diligence (ESDD).
